lessons.title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
lessons.description: What affects the speed of chemical reactions, and how collision theory explains reaction rates.
lessons.content_html:
Rate of Reaction

The rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are turned into products. It can be calculated by:

$$\text{rate of reaction} = \frac{\text{quantity of reactant used or product formed}}{\text{time taken}}$$

The rate of a chemical reaction can be changed by altering the: temperature, concentration of solutions (or pressure of gases), surface area of solid reactants, or by using a catalyst.

Key Fact

Rate of reaction can be increased by: raising temperature, increasing concentration/pressure, increasing surface area, or using a catalyst. The rate can be measured by collecting gas, measuring mass loss, or timing colour changes.

Collision Theory

Collision theory states that for a reaction to occur, particles must: (1) collide with each other, and (2) collide with sufficient energy. The minimum energy needed for a successful collision is called the activation energy.

Each factor affects the rate by changing the frequency or energy of collisions:

  • Temperature — higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy \(\geq\) activation energy.
  • Concentration / Pressure — more particles in the same volume means more frequent collisions.
  • Surface area — smaller pieces expose more surface, giving more area for collisions to occur.
  • Catalyst — provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful. The catalyst is not used up.
Key Fact

Collision theory: reactions only happen when particles collide with energy ≥ activation energy. Catalysts lower the activation energy — they are not used up and do not appear in the overall equation.

Common methods for measuring rate include: collecting gas in a gas syringe or over water, measuring the loss of mass on a balance (when gas escapes), or timing how long it takes for a solution to become opaque (e.g. sodium thiosulfate "disappearing cross" experiment). On a graph, a steeper curve means a faster rate.

On a graph of volume of gas vs time: the gradient (steepness) at any point represents the rate. A steeper line = faster rate. The line levels off when the reaction is complete (one reactant has been used up). Changing temperature or concentration affects the steepness but not the final volume (if the same amount of reactant is used). Increasing the amount of reactant increases the total gas produced.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining why a factor changes the rate, always use collision theory language: “more frequent collisions” or “more particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.” Simply saying “particles move faster” is not enough for full marks — you must link to collision frequency and energy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rate of reaction = quantity of product formed or reactant used ÷ time.
  • Collision theory: particles must collide with energy ≥ activation energy. More frequent/energetic collisions = faster rate.
  • Catalysts lower the activation energy without being used up; temperature, concentration, surface area all increase collision frequency.

lessons.title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium
lessons.description: How some reactions can go in both directions, and what happens at dynamic equilibrium.
lessons.content_html:
Reversible Reactions

Some chemical reactions are reversible — the products can react to re-form the original reactants. A reversible reaction is shown with a double arrow (\(\rightleftharpoons\)):

$$A + B \rightleftharpoons C + D$$

A simple example is the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride:

$$NH_4Cl \rightleftharpoons NH_3 + HCl$$

When heated, ammonium chloride decomposes into ammonia and hydrogen chloride. When cooled, these gases recombine to form ammonium chloride again.

Key Fact

In a reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic by the same amount of energy, and vice versa.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction occurs in a closed system (where nothing can enter or leave), it eventually reaches dynamic equilibrium. At equilibrium:

  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but are not necessarily equal).
  • The reaction has not stopped — both forward and reverse reactions are still occurring.

If conditions are changed, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change (Le Chatelier’s principle):

  • Temperature: Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • Concentration: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products. Increasing the concentration of a product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Pressure (gases only): Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas.

A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, helping equilibrium to be reached faster.

Key Fact

Le Chatelier’s principle: if conditions change, equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Catalysts speed up both reactions equally — they do not change the equilibrium position.

The Haber process manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen:

$$N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3$$

The forward reaction is exothermic. Conditions used: temperature of about 450°C, pressure of about 200 atmospheres, and an iron catalyst. The temperature is a compromise — lower temperature would give a higher yield but the rate would be too slow. The iron catalyst speeds up the reaction without changing the yield.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When predicting how a change in conditions affects equilibrium, always state: (1) which direction the equilibrium shifts, (2) why it shifts (to oppose the change), and (3) the effect on the yield of products. For the Haber process, explain why a compromise temperature is used — not just what the conditions are.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reversible reactions go in both directions; if forward is exothermic, reverse is endothermic (same energy).
  • At dynamic equilibrium (closed system): forward rate = reverse rate; concentrations constant but not necessarily equal.
  • Le Chatelier’s principle: equilibrium shifts to oppose changes in temperature, concentration or pressure. Catalysts don’t change position.

lessons.title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons and Cracking
lessons.description: How crude oil is separated by fractional distillation, alkane properties, and cracking.
lessons.content_html:
Crude Oil and Hydrocarbons

Crude oil is a finite resource formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient marine organisms. It is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons (molecules containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms).

The hydrocarbons in crude oil are separated by fractional distillation. The crude oil is heated until most of it evaporates. The vapours rise up a tall column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top. Different fractions condense at different heights depending on their boiling points: smaller molecules condense near the top (low boiling point) and larger molecules condense near the bottom (high boiling point).

Key Fact

Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation. Smaller hydrocarbons have lower boiling points, are less viscous, more flammable, and are collected near the top of the column. Larger hydrocarbons have higher boiling points and are collected near the bottom.

Alkanes

Most hydrocarbons in crude oil are alkanes. They have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n+2}\). The first four are:

  • Methane: \(CH_4\)
  • Ethane: \(C_2H_6\)
  • Propane: \(C_3H_8\)
  • Butane: \(C_4H_{10}\)

As the carbon chain gets longer: boiling point increases, viscosity increases (thicker), and flammability decreases (harder to ignite). These trends are due to stronger intermolecular forces between the larger molecules.

Hydrocarbons are used as fuels because they release energy when burned (combustion). Complete combustion (plenty of oxygen) produces carbon dioxide and water:

$$CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O$$

Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) produces carbon monoxide (toxic) and/or carbon (soot), as well as water. Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it is colourless, odourless, and binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport.

Cracking

Cracking is the process of breaking down long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful molecules. There is more demand for shorter-chain hydrocarbons (fuels like petrol) than for longer-chain ones. Cracking also produces alkenes, which are used to make polymers and other chemicals.

Key Fact

Cracking: long alkane → shorter alkane + alkene. Methods: catalytic cracking (hot catalyst) or steam cracking (high temperature + steam). Alkenes have a C=C double bond and are used to make polymers.

Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond (\(C=C\)) and have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n}\). They are described as unsaturated. You can test for the presence of a \(C=C\) double bond using bromine water: it turns from orange to colourless with an alkene (the bromine adds across the double bond). Alkanes do not decolourise bromine water because they are saturated (no double bonds).
lessons.exam_tip_html: Make sure you can explain the trends in properties as chain length increases and link them to intermolecular forces. For cracking, always give both types of products (a shorter alkane AND an alkene). The bromine water test is a favourite exam question — state the colour change (orange to colourless) and what it shows (presence of a C=C double bond).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation based on boiling points; smaller molecules collect at the top.
  • Alkanes: \(C_nH_{2n+2}\), saturated, single bonds. As chain length increases: BP increases, viscosity increases, flammability decreases.
  • Cracking breaks long alkanes into shorter alkanes + alkenes. Bromine water test: orange → colourless = alkene present.

lessons.title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests
lessons.description: How chemists test for purity, use chromatography, and identify common gases.
lessons.content_html:
Pure Substances and Mixtures

In chemistry, a pure substance consists of a single element or compound. It has a sharp, fixed melting point and boiling point. A mixture contains two or more substances not chemically combined. Mixtures melt over a range of temperatures rather than at a sharp point.

Key Fact

A pure substance has a sharp, specific melting point. An impure substance / mixture melts over a range of temperatures. You can test purity by checking the melting point against the known value.

Chromatography

Chromatography is used to separate and identify substances in a mixture. In paper chromatography, a spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line on chromatography paper. The paper is placed in a solvent. As the solvent moves up the paper, it carries the dissolved substances with it. Different substances travel different distances depending on their solubility.

The R\(_f\) value is calculated as:

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}}$$

Each substance has a unique \(R_f\) value in a given solvent. A pure substance produces a single spot; a mixture produces multiple spots.

You can identify substances by comparing their \(R_f\) values with known reference values, or by running known substances alongside the unknown on the same chromatogram. If a spot in the unknown lines up exactly with a spot from a known substance, they are the same compound.

Tests for Common Gases

You need to know the tests for four gases:

Key Fact

Gas tests: Hydrogen — squeaky pop with a lighted splint. Oxygen — relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide — turns limewater milky/cloudy. Chlorine — bleaches damp litmus paper white.

A formulation is a mixture designed as a useful product, where each component is present in a measured quantity to give it specific properties. Examples include medicines (active ingredient + binder + coating), paints (pigment + solvent + binder), and alloys (metals mixed in specific ratios for desired properties).

Formulations are found everywhere in everyday life. Each ingredient has a specific purpose, and changing the proportions changes the properties of the product.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When calculating \(R_f\) values, always measure from the pencil baseline (not the bottom of the paper) to the centre of the spot. Show your working clearly. Remember that \(R_f\) values are always between 0 and 1. For gas test questions, state both the test AND the positive result.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pure substances have sharp melting/boiling points; impure substances melt over a range.
  • Chromatography separates mixtures; \(R_f\) values identify substances. Pure = one spot, mixture = multiple spots.
  • Gas tests: hydrogen (squeaky pop), oxygen (relights splint), CO\(_2\) (limewater milky), chlorine (bleaches litmus).

lessons.title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect
lessons.description: How the atmosphere evolved over billions of years and how greenhouse gases cause climate change.
lessons.content_html:
The Early Atmosphere

For the first billion years, the Earth’s atmosphere was very different from today. Scientists believe it was mainly carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen — similar to the atmospheres of Venus and Mars today. There was also water vapour, nitrogen and small amounts of methane and ammonia. This early atmosphere was produced by volcanic activity.

The water vapour condensed as the Earth cooled, forming the oceans. Over billions of years, the atmosphere changed dramatically:

Step 1: The first simple organisms (algae and photosynthetic bacteria) evolved in the oceans. They used \(CO_2\) for photosynthesis and released \(O_2\), gradually increasing the oxygen level in the atmosphere.

Step 2: \(CO_2\) was also removed by dissolving in the oceans, where it formed carbonates in sedimentary rocks and the shells/skeletons of marine organisms.

Step 3: As \(O_2\) levels increased, more complex life evolved. The ozone layer (\(O_3\)) formed, shielding life from UV radiation.

Key Fact

Today’s atmosphere: approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus small amounts of other gases (argon, water vapour). This has been roughly stable for 200 million years.

The Greenhouse Effect

Greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) absorb heat radiation (infrared) from the Earth’s surface and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards Earth. This natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough to support life.

However, human activities are increasing the concentrations of greenhouse gases:

  • Carbon dioxide — burning fossil fuels, deforestation.
  • Methane — agriculture (cattle farming, rice paddies), landfill sites.

This enhanced greenhouse effect is causing global warming — an increase in global average temperatures. The consequences include: sea level rise (thermal expansion and melting ice), more extreme weather events, changes to ecosystems and species distribution, and impacts on agriculture.

Key Fact

Human activities increase \(CO_2\) (fossil fuels, deforestation) and \(CH_4\) (farming, landfill). Enhanced greenhouse effect → global warming → rising sea levels, extreme weather, habitat loss.

A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gases released over the life cycle of a product or activity. It can be reduced by: using renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, carbon capture and storage, reducing meat consumption, and reducing travel.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked about atmospheric change, use a timeline: early atmosphere (mostly \(CO_2\), volcanic) → algae evolved (photosynthesis added \(O_2\), removed \(CO_2\)) → today (78% \(N_2\), 21% \(O_2\)). For greenhouse effect questions, always describe the mechanism: greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Early atmosphere: mostly \(CO_2\) from volcanoes. Photosynthesis by algae added \(O_2\) and removed \(CO_2\) over billions of years.
  • Today’s atmosphere: ~78% nitrogen, ~21% oxygen, ~0.04% \(CO_2\).
  • Human activities increase greenhouse gases, enhancing the greenhouse effect and causing global warming.

lessons.title: Atmospheric Pollutants and Their Effects
lessons.description: How burning fuels produces pollutants, and their effects on health and the environment.
lessons.content_html:
Pollutants from Fuels

When fossil fuels are burned, several pollutant gases can be released into the atmosphere. The type and amount of pollutant depends on the fuel and the conditions of combustion.

The main pollutants are:

  • Carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)) — produced by complete combustion of any hydrocarbon. A greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming.
  • Carbon monoxide (\(CO\)) — produced by incomplete combustion. A toxic, colourless, odourless gas that binds to haemoglobin in the blood, preventing it from carrying oxygen. Can cause death.
  • Soot / particulates (carbon particles) — also from incomplete combustion. Cause respiratory problems, make buildings dirty, and contribute to global dimming (blocking sunlight).
  • Sulfur dioxide (\(SO_2\)) — produced when fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned. Causes acid rain, which damages buildings (corrodes limestone/marble), kills trees and acidifies lakes.
  • Nitrogen oxides (\(NO_x\)) — formed when nitrogen and oxygen react at the high temperatures inside car engines. Also cause acid rain and respiratory problems.
Key Fact

Fossil fuel pollutants: \(CO_2\) (greenhouse gas), CO (toxic), soot (respiratory problems), \(SO_2\) (acid rain from sulfur impurities), \(NO_x\) (acid rain from high temperature reaction of \(N_2\) and \(O_2\)).

Reducing Pollution

Catalytic converters in car exhausts convert toxic carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into less harmful gases:

$$2CO + 2NO \rightarrow 2CO_2 + N_2$$

Flue gas desulfurisation removes \(SO_2\) from power station emissions by reacting it with calcium oxide or calcium carbonate, producing calcium sulfate (which can be used to make plaster).

Key Fact

Solutions: catalytic converters reduce CO and \(NO_x\), flue gas desulfurisation removes \(SO_2\). Using low-sulfur fuels, renewable energy, and electric vehicles also reduces pollution.

Air pollution is a global issue. Pollutants can travel long distances in the atmosphere, meaning emissions in one country can cause acid rain in another. International agreements (such as the Paris Agreement) aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Developing countries face challenges balancing economic growth with pollution reduction.

Alternative approaches to reducing pollution include: switching to renewable energy sources (wind, solar, hydroelectric), using electric or hydrogen-powered vehicles, improving fuel efficiency, and developing carbon capture and storage technologies.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining how a pollutant is formed, always state the specific conditions. For example: \(NO_x\) forms at the high temperatures inside engines where \(N_2\) and \(O_2\) react; \(SO_2\) forms when sulfur impurities in the fuel burn. Don’t confuse incomplete combustion products (CO, soot) with products of complete combustion (\(CO_2\), \(H_2O\)).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Burning fossil fuels produces pollutants: \(CO_2\) (global warming), CO (toxic), soot (respiratory), \(SO_2\) and \(NO_x\) (acid rain).
  • CO and \(NO_x\) are reduced by catalytic converters; \(SO_2\) is removed by flue gas desulfurisation.
  • Long-term solutions include renewable energy, electric vehicles, and carbon capture and storage.

lessons.title: Using Earth's Resources and Sustainability
lessons.description: How we use natural resources, potable water treatment, and sustainable development.
lessons.content_html:
Natural Resources and Products

Humans use the Earth’s natural resources to provide warmth, shelter, food, and transport. Some resources are finite (non-renewable) — they will eventually run out (e.g. fossil fuels, metal ores). Others are renewable — they can be replaced (e.g. timber, cotton).

Sustainable development means meeting the needs of today’s population without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs. Chemistry plays a vital role in sustainable development by finding alternatives to finite resources and reducing waste.

Key Fact

Sustainable development: meet today’s needs without compromising the future. Strategies include using renewable resources, recycling, reducing waste, and developing new materials (e.g. bioplastics).

Potable Water

Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It is not the same as pure water — it contains low levels of dissolved substances. In the UK, potable water is produced from fresh water (rivers, reservoirs) by:

  1. Filtration — passing through filter beds to remove large debris, gravel and sand.
  2. Sedimentation — allowing fine particles to settle out.
  3. Sterilisation — adding chlorine, or using UV light or ozone to kill bacteria and make water safe.

In areas with limited fresh water, sea water can be made potable by desalination. Methods include distillation (boiling the water and condensing the steam) and reverse osmosis (forcing water through a membrane that blocks salt). Both methods require significant energy, making them expensive.

Key Fact

UK potable water: fresh water → filtration → sedimentation → sterilisation (chlorine/UV/ozone). Desalination converts sea water but requires a lot of energy. Potable ≠ pure — it still contains some dissolved substances.

Waste Water Treatment

Waste water (sewage and industrial water) must be treated before release into the environment. The process includes:

Screening: large objects (rags, sticks) are removed by passing water through screens.

Sedimentation: solids settle out as sludge. The liquid effluent is separated.

Biological treatment: aerobic bacteria break down organic matter in the effluent. The sludge is also digested anaerobically by bacteria, producing biogas (methane) which can be used as fuel.

Final treatment: the cleaned water is tested and released back into rivers or the sea.

Life Cycle Assessments and Recycling

A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage: extracting raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, and disposal (landfill, recycling, or incineration). LCAs help companies make products more sustainable.

Reducing, reusing and recycling materials conserves finite resources, reduces energy consumption, and decreases the amount of waste going to landfill. However, recycling has its own costs (collection, sorting, processing energy) and LCAs can be subjective.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Remember that potable water is NOT the same as pure water. In the exam, you may be asked to compare the processes for producing potable water from fresh water vs sea water. The key difference is that desalination (from sea water) requires much more energy because dissolved salts must be removed, whereas fresh water treatment mainly removes debris and pathogens.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sustainable development balances current needs with future resources; chemistry develops alternatives to finite resources.
  • Potable water: filtration → sedimentation → sterilisation. Desalination for sea water (energy-intensive).
  • Life cycle assessments evaluate environmental impact at every stage; reduce, reuse, recycle to conserve resources.

lessons.title: Alkenes, Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids
lessons.description: The structure, properties, and reactions of alkenes, alcohols, and carboxylic acids.
lessons.content_html:
Alkenes

Alkenes are a homologous series of hydrocarbons that contain a carbon–carbon double bond (\(\text{C}=\text{C}\)). This double bond makes them unsaturated — they have fewer hydrogen atoms than the equivalent alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.

Key Fact

The general formula for alkenes is \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\). The first three members are: ethene (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\)), propene (\(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\)), and butene (\(\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\)). Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) double bond.

Test for alkenes: Add bromine water (orange) to the substance. If an alkene is present, the bromine water is decolourised (turns colourless) because bromine adds across the double bond in an addition reaction. Alkanes do not decolourise bromine water because they have no double bonds.

Alkenes undergo addition reactions because the double bond can open up and bond with other atoms:

  • With hydrogen (hydrogenation): Produces an alkane. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6\) (using a nickel catalyst at 150 °C).
  • With water/steam (hydration): Produces an alcohol. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\).
  • With bromine: Produces a dibromo compound. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Br}_2\).

Alcohols

Alcohols contain the functional group \(-\text{OH}\) (hydroxyl group). The general formula is \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+1}\text{OH}\). The first three members are methanol (\(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\)), ethanol (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\)), and propanol (\(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}\)).

Combustion: Alcohols burn in air to produce carbon dioxide and water. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\). This makes them useful as fuels (e.g. ethanol as a biofuel).

With sodium: Alcohols react with sodium metal to produce hydrogen gas and a sodium alkoxide. \(2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2\). This reaction is less vigorous than sodium with water.

Oxidation: Alcohols can be oxidised to form carboxylic acids. This happens when ethanol is left exposed to air (bacterial oxidation turns wine into vinegar), or when an acidified potassium dichromate solution is heated with the alcohol — the solution changes from orange to green.

Key Fact

Ethanol is produced in two ways: (1) Fermentation of sugars using yeast at 25–30 °C in anaerobic conditions (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{CO}_2\)), and (2) Hydration of ethene with steam using a phosphoric acid catalyst at 300 °C and 60–70 atm.

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain the functional group \(-\text{COOH}\) (carboxyl group). The first three members are methanoic acid (\(\text{HCOOH}\)), ethanoic acid (\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)), and propanoic acid (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}\)).

Carboxylic acids are weak acids — they do not fully dissociate (ionise) in water. This means a solution of ethanoic acid has a higher pH (is less acidic) than a solution of hydrochloric acid at the same concentration.

Carboxylic acids react like other acids:

  • With metal carbonates: Produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide. \(2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\)
  • With alcohols: Produce an ester and water in a condensation reaction (requires an acid catalyst). \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Esters often have fruity smells and are used in flavourings and perfumes.

Key Fact

The three homologous series are linked: alkenes can be hydrated to make alcohols, and alcohols can be oxidised to make carboxylic acids. Understanding these links helps you see how organic chemistry fits together.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The bromine water test is a very common exam question — always state that the bromine water changes from orange to colourless (not “clear”, which could mean transparent). For carboxylic acids, remember they are weak acids (partially dissociate), not dilute — weak and dilute are different concepts. If asked to write the formula of an ester, remember the pattern: acid name first + alcohol name (e.g. ethanoic acid + methanol = methyl ethanoate).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Alkenes contain a \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) double bond, are unsaturated (general formula \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\)), and decolourise bromine water through addition reactions.
  • Alcohols contain the \(-\text{OH}\) group, burn as fuels, react with sodium, and can be oxidised to carboxylic acids.
  • Carboxylic acids contain \(-\text{COOH}\), are weak acids (partially dissociate), and react with alcohols to form esters.

lessons.title: Polymers: Addition, Condensation and Natural
lessons.description: How addition and condensation polymers form, plus natural polymers like DNA and proteins.
lessons.content_html:
Polymers

Polymers are very large molecules made by linking together thousands of small molecules called monomers. The process of joining monomers together is called polymerisation. For separate chemistry, you need to understand two types: addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.

Addition Polymers

Addition polymerisation occurs when many unsaturated monomer molecules (alkenes) join together. The double bond (\(\text{C}=\text{C}\)) in each monomer “opens up” and bonds to the next monomer, forming a long saturated chain. No other product is formed — the only product is the polymer.

Key Fact

In addition polymerisation, the monomer must contain a \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) double bond. The polymer has a \(\text{C}-\text{C}\) single bond backbone. The atom economy is 100% because no by-products are formed. Example: ethene (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\)) polymerises to form poly(ethene).

Common addition polymers include:

  • Poly(ethene) — from ethene. Used for plastic bags, bottles, and packaging.
  • Poly(propene) — from propene. Used for ropes, carpets, and food containers.
  • Poly(chloroethene) (PVC) — from chloroethene. Used for window frames, pipes, and flooring.
  • PTFE (Teflon) — from tetrafluoroethene. Used for non-stick coatings on pans.

Condensation Polymers

Condensation polymerisation is different from addition polymerisation. It occurs when monomers with two functional groups join together, and a small molecule (usually water) is released at each link.

Key Fact

Condensation polymerisation produces a polymer plus a small molecule (usually \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\)). This means the atom economy is less than 100%. The two main types of condensation polymer are polyesters (from a dicarboxylic acid + a diol) and polyamides (from a dicarboxylic acid + a diamine).

Polyesters are formed when a dicarboxylic acid (with two \(-\text{COOH}\) groups) reacts with a diol (with two \(-\text{OH}\) groups). An ester link (\(-\text{COO}-\)) forms between each pair, and water is released. Example: PET (polyethylene terephthalate), used in plastic bottles and clothing fibres.

Polyamides are formed when a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diamine (with two \(-\text{NH}_2\) groups). An amide link (\(-\text{CONH}-\)) forms between each pair, and water is released. Example: nylon, used in ropes, clothing, and engineering plastics.

Natural Polymers

Many biological molecules are natural polymers formed by condensation polymerisation:

Proteins are natural polyamides. They are made from amino acid monomers joined by peptide bonds (a type of amide link). Each amino acid has both an amine group (\(-\text{NH}_2\)) and a carboxyl group (\(-\text{COOH}\)), so they can form long chains through condensation reactions.

DNA is a natural polymer made from nucleotide monomers. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group, and a base. The nucleotides are linked by condensation reactions between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next.

Starch and cellulose are natural polymers of glucose (a sugar monomer). Starch is used for energy storage in plants, while cellulose provides structural support in plant cell walls.

Addition: Monomers must have \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) double bonds. Only one product (the polymer). 100% atom economy. Examples: poly(ethene), PVC.

Condensation: Monomers must have two functional groups. Two products (polymer + water). Less than 100% atom economy. Examples: polyester (PET), nylon, proteins, DNA.

Key Fact

You can identify the type of polymerisation from the polymer structure: if the polymer backbone contains only \(\text{C}-\text{C}\) bonds, it is an addition polymer. If the backbone contains ester links (\(-\text{COO}-\)) or amide links (\(-\text{CONH}-\)), it is a condensation polymer.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A very common exam question gives you a section of a polymer and asks you to identify the monomer(s) and the type of polymerisation. For addition polymers, look for a \(\text{C}-\text{C}\) backbone and add a double bond back between the two carbons in the repeating unit. For condensation polymers, look for ester or amide links — insert \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) across the link to recover the two monomers. Always state whether water is lost.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Addition polymerisation uses alkene monomers (\(\text{C}=\text{C}\)), produces only the polymer, and has 100% atom economy.
  • Condensation polymerisation uses monomers with two functional groups, produces a polymer plus water, and has less than 100% atom economy. It forms polyesters and polyamides.
  • Natural polymers (proteins, DNA, starch) are also formed by condensation reactions from biological monomers.

lessons.title: Chemical Tests for Ions
lessons.description: How to identify metal ions, non-metal ions, and gases using standard chemical tests.
lessons.content_html:
Testing for Ions

In separate chemistry, you need to know how to identify unknown substances using a range of chemical tests. These tests are based on characteristic reactions that produce observable results — colour changes, precipitates, or gas production.

Flame Tests for Metal Ions

A flame test identifies metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen flame. A clean nichrome wire loop is dipped in the sample, then held in the blue flame.

Key Fact

Flame test colours: Lithium = crimson red. Sodium = yellow. Potassium = lilac. Calcium = orange-red. Copper = green.

Testing with Sodium Hydroxide Solution

Adding a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution to a solution containing metal ions produces a coloured precipitate (an insoluble solid). The colour of the precipitate identifies the metal ion:

  • Calcium (Ca²+): white precipitate.
  • Magnesium (Mg²+): white precipitate.
  • Aluminium (Al³+): white precipitate — but dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution.
  • Copper(II) (Cu²+): blue precipitate.
  • Iron(II) (Fe²+): green precipitate.
  • Iron(III) (Fe³+): brown precipitate.

Calcium, magnesium, and aluminium all produce white precipitates with NaOH. To distinguish between them:

  • Aluminium dissolves in excess NaOH (the white precipitate disappears). Calcium and magnesium do not.
  • Calcium can be confirmed by a flame test (orange-red flame). Magnesium does not produce a visible flame colour.

Testing for Negative Ions (Anions)

Testing for carbonates (\(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\)): Add dilute acid to the sample. If carbonate ions are present, the mixture fizzes and produces carbon dioxide gas, which turns limewater milky (cloudy).

Testing for halide ions (\(\text{Cl}^-\), \(\text{Br}^-\), \(\text{I}^-\)): Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution. The colour of the precipitate identifies the halide:

  • Chloride: white precipitate (silver chloride).
  • Bromide: cream precipitate (silver bromide).
  • Iodide: yellow precipitate (silver iodide).

Testing for sulfate ions (\(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\)): Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms if sulfate ions are present.

Key Fact

The acid is added first in halide and sulfate tests to remove any carbonate ions that might otherwise interfere with the results by forming precipitates of their own.

Tests for Gases

You also need to know how to test for common gases:

  • Hydrogen (\(\text{H}_2\)): Hold a burning splint near the gas. It burns with a squeaky pop.
  • Oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)): Insert a glowing splint into the gas. It relights.
  • Carbon dioxide (\(\text{CO}_2\)): Bubble through limewater. It turns milky/cloudy.
  • Chlorine (\(\text{Cl}_2\)): Hold damp litmus paper near the gas. It bleaches the litmus paper white.

Modern laboratories use instrumental methods of analysis that are more sensitive, faster, and can handle very small samples. Examples include spectroscopy and chromatography. These methods are particularly useful for detecting trace amounts of substances or for analysing complex mixtures.

Key Fact

Instrumental methods of analysis are preferred over chemical tests in industry because they are more accurate, more sensitive (can detect smaller amounts), faster, and require smaller sample sizes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Learn the flame test colours as a list — they are frequently tested. For precipitate tests, always state the colour of the precipitate, not just that a precipitate forms. Remember: to test for halides use silver nitrate (with nitric acid first), and to test for sulfates use barium chloride (with hydrochloric acid first). A common mistake is mixing up which reagent goes with which test.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Flame tests identify metal ions by colour: Li (crimson), Na (yellow), K (lilac), Ca (orange-red), Cu (green).
  • NaOH solution produces coloured precipitates: Cu2+ (blue), Fe2+ (green), Fe3+ (brown), Ca/Mg/Al (white, with Al dissolving in excess).
  • Halides are tested with silver nitrate (Cl− white, Br− cream, I− yellow). Sulfates are tested with barium chloride (white precipitate). Gases have specific tests (squeaky pop, relights splint, limewater, bleaches litmus).

lessons.title: Materials, Corrosion, Haber Process and Fertilisers
lessons.description: Corrosion and alloys, the Haber process for ammonia, and NPK fertiliser production.
lessons.content_html:
Corrosion

Corrosion is the destruction of metals by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. The most familiar example is rusting, which occurs when iron reacts with both oxygen and water.

Key Fact

Rusting requires both oxygen and water. If either is absent, iron will not rust. The word equation is: iron + water + oxygen → hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Rusting is an oxidation reaction because the iron is oxidised.

Corrosion can be prevented in several ways:

  • Painting, greasing, or oiling — creates a physical barrier that prevents oxygen and water reaching the metal surface.
  • Galvanising — coating iron with a layer of zinc. Even if the zinc coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially because it is more reactive than iron (sacrificial protection).
  • Electroplating — using electrolysis to coat a metal with a thin layer of a more attractive or less reactive metal (e.g. chromium plating on car parts).

Most metals used in everyday life are alloys — mixtures of metals (or a metal with a non-metal). Alloys are harder and stronger than pure metals because atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, preventing them from sliding over each other easily.

Examples of alloys:

  • Steel — iron + carbon (and sometimes other metals). Low carbon steel is easy to shape; high carbon steel is hard; stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel) resists corrosion.
  • Bronze — copper + tin. Hard and resistant to corrosion.
  • Brass — copper + zinc. Easy to shape and has a gold-like appearance.

The Haber Process

The Haber process is one of the most important industrial chemical processes. It produces ammonia (\(\text{NH}_3\)) from nitrogen (from the air) and hydrogen (from natural gas or steam reforming).

Key Fact

The Haber process equation: \(\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3\). Conditions: temperature of 450 °C, pressure of 200 atmospheres, and an iron catalyst. The reaction is reversible, so these conditions are a compromise to give a reasonable yield at a reasonable rate.

The forward reaction (making ammonia) is exothermic. By Le Chatelier's principle:

  • Temperature: A lower temperature would give a higher yield (favours the exothermic forward reaction), but the rate would be too slow. 450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate.
  • Pressure: Higher pressure gives a higher yield (fewer gas molecules on the product side: 4 moles of reactants → 2 moles of products). 200 atm is used because very high pressures are expensive and dangerous.
  • Iron catalyst: Speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, helping the reaction reach equilibrium faster. It does not change the yield, only the rate.

Any unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back through the reactor to maximise overall conversion.

Fertilisers

NPK fertilisers provide the three essential elements that plants need for growth: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). Ammonia from the Haber process is a key starting material for nitrogen-containing fertilisers.

The production of NPK fertilisers involves several steps:

  • Ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate (\(\text{NH}_3 + \text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3\)) — provides nitrogen.
  • Ammonia + sulfuric acid → ammonium sulfate — another nitrogen source.
  • Phosphate rock + acid → soluble phosphates — provides phosphorus.
  • Potassium chloride or potassium sulfate — provides potassium (mined from mineral deposits).
Key Fact

Plants need nitrogen to make proteins and chlorophyll, phosphorus for DNA and energy transfer, and potassium for enzyme function and disease resistance. Without fertilisers, crop yields would be significantly lower.

NPK fertilisers can be formulated in the laboratory by reacting an acid with an alkali to produce a soluble salt. The proportions of N, P, and K can be adjusted to suit different crops and soil conditions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the Haber process, you must be able to explain why each condition is chosen, not just state the values. Always link back to Le Chatelier’s principle and explain the compromise between yield and rate. For corrosion questions, remember that rusting requires both oxygen and water — this is a very common mark. When describing sacrificial protection, explain that the more reactive metal corrodes instead of the iron.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rusting requires both oxygen and water. It can be prevented by barriers (paint, grease), galvanising (sacrificial protection with zinc), or electroplating.
  • The Haber process makes ammonia: \(\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3\) at 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst — a compromise between yield and rate.
  • NPK fertilisers provide nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium for plant growth. Ammonia is the starting material for nitrogen fertilisers like ammonium nitrate.

practice_questions.text: Name the two substances that must both be present for iron to rust.
practice_questions.marks: Oxygen and water (1 mark for both).

practice_questions.text: Describe how galvanising protects iron from rusting.
practice_questions.marks: Iron is coated with a layer of zinc (1 mark). Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes/reacts preferentially (sacrificial protection), protecting the iron even if the coating is scratched (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: In the Haber process, 28 tonnes of nitrogen reacts with excess hydrogen. Calculate the maximum mass of ammonia that could be produced. (Ar: N = 14, H = 1)
practice_questions.marks:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Mr of N₂ = 28, Mr of 2NH₃ = 2 × 17 = 34.
28 tonnes of N₂ produces 34 tonnes of NH₃ (1 mark for method, 1 mark for answer = 34 tonnes).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Haber process uses a temperature of 450 °C rather than a lower temperature.
practice_questions.marks: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would increase the yield of ammonia (1 mark). However, a lower temperature would make the rate of reaction too slow (1 mark). 450 °C is a compromise that gives a reasonable yield at a reasonable rate (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Compare the effectiveness of painting and galvanising as methods of preventing iron from rusting.
practice_questions.marks: Both methods create a barrier between the iron and oxygen/water (1 mark). If the paint is scratched, the iron underneath is exposed and can rust (1 mark). If the zinc coating in galvanising is scratched, the zinc still protects the iron by sacrificial protection because zinc is more reactive (1 mark). Galvanising is therefore more effective for objects that may be scratched or damaged (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: The Haber process is essential for modern agriculture. Evaluate the importance of the Haber process for food production, considering both the benefits and environmental concerns of using nitrogen fertilisers.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed evaluation of the Haber process's role in food production with specific links to fertilisers, alongside environmental concerns, with a balanced conclusion.
Mid band (3-4): Describes benefits of ammonia/fertilisers and some environmental concerns. May lack specific detail.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements about fertilisers being useful or harmful.
Indicative content:
• Benefits: ammonia from Haber process is used to make nitrogen fertilisers (ammonium nitrate); these increase crop yields dramatically; essential for feeding the growing global population; estimates suggest Haber process supports food production for ~50% of world population
• Environmental concerns: excess fertiliser runs off into rivers/lakes causing eutrophication (algal blooms, oxygen depletion); manufacturing ammonia requires large amounts of energy (usually from fossil fuels); hydrogen for the process often comes from natural gas (non-renewable)
• The process conditions (450°C, 200 atm) require significant energy input
• Unreacted gases are recycled to improve efficiency
• Conclusion should weigh the essential role in food security against environmental costs

glossary_terms.definition: The gradual destruction of a metal by chemical reactions with substances in its environment, such as oxygen and water.
The corrosion of iron in the presence of both oxygen and water, forming hydrated iron(III) oxide.
A reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen, losing electrons in the process.
A method of rust prevention where a more reactive metal corrodes instead of the iron, protecting it even if the coating is damaged.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, designed to have improved properties such as greater strength or resistance to corrosion.
The industrial process for producing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, using high temperature, high pressure, and an iron catalyst.
A compound of nitrogen and hydrogen (NH₃) used to make fertilisers, explosives, and many other chemicals.
Fertilisers containing nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K), the three essential elements that plants need for healthy growth.
